summary.name: Sustainable On-Call
summary.one_liner: A 2018 blog essay by Cody Wilbourn arguing that on-call burnout comes mainly from alert frequency and alert volume, and laying out human and technical strategies to reduce both.
use_cases: Reducing on-call alert noise on a monitoring setup
Deciding whether to hire more on-call staff or use follow-the-sun coverage
Designing compensation time policy after incidents
Tuning monitors so each alert requires action
Preventing cascading failures from flooding on-call with alerts
Structuring primary and secondary on-call roles
summary.what_it_does: The essay argues that the worst part of on-call comes from how often alerts arrive (frequency) and how many arrive at once during incidents (volume). For frequency, it discusses human strategies such as compensation time and hiring (including follow-the-sun coverage and 24x7 help desks), and technical strategies such as making alerts actionable, removing false positives, and fixing the systems that generate repeated alerts. For volume, it recommends prioritizing monitors, alerting on the worst value of a metric rather than every partition or instance, reducing overlapping monitors, and designing systems to degrade gracefully (redundancy, caching, read replicas, retry backoff, circuit breakers, feature flags). It also suggests a secondary on-call engineer for complex incidents. The closing argues that culture and sustainability matter more than any single fix.
notable: Splits on-call stress into frequency and volume, and maps each to specific human and technical fixes
Describes a 'worst value' composite monitor approach for prioritizing alerts during outages
Explains follow-the-sun staffing and 24x7 help desk as staffing options
caveats: Opinion essay based on the author's personal experience; it gives no quantitative data
Does not offer a copy-and-paste on-call policy; the author says answers vary by company
